lesson:
The AI project cycle is a framework providing a sequence of steps to tackle an artificial intelligence challenge. It consists of six distinct stages: problem scoping, data acquisition, data exploration, modeling, evaluation, and deployment.

Problem scoping is considered the most important step in the AI project cycle. In this stage, you determine success and goal definitions by starting with the end in mind. To ensure problem definitions are as complete as possible, the four Ws framework is used: Who, What, Where, and Why. "Who" identifies the stakeholders and beneficiaries facing the problem. "What" explores the nature of the problem and the evidence proving it exists. "Where" looks at the context or time perspective in which the problem arises. "Why" defines the motivation, value proposition, and the safety or benefits of solving the problem. Examples of scoped problems include drowsy bus drivers and detecting fraud on e-commerce websites.

Data acquisition involves finding and collecting appropriate data for the AI project. Data can come from internal origin points, such as an e-commerce website's activity, or from public domain sources and organizations. Examples of data sources include Kaggle, a platform for AI and data science work to publish and find datasets; Amazon Web Services (AWS), which provides a registry of open data; the World Bank, which makes national and international data available regarding health, education, and nutrition; and the United States government, which provides population datasets.

Data exploration is the data science aspect where the raw dataset is examined from different perspectives to see how it can best be used to solve the problem. Because raw numbers can be overwhelming, visualization tools like Power BI and Tableau are generally used to turn raw numbers into charts, graphs, and aggregate views that help humans easily recognize patterns and big-picture characteristics.

Modeling is where the heavy lifting of the AI occurs. It involves creating a mathematical algorithm or program based on data to interact with and make sense of new data it has not seen before. Machine learning serves as the primary modeling technique, where feeding data into a model acts like an accelerated experience. Machine learning models are divided into three main families: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. Supervised learning determines relationships through training on known labeled data, where every data point is categorized into a class associated with a fixed mark by a human. Sub-techniques of supervised learning include classification, which predicts categorical data (qualitative characteristics or classes such as identifying whether an image contains a fox), and regression, which predicts numerical data (quantitative measurements or values such as housing prices). Unsupervised learning discovers patterns and relationships by traversing through large amounts of unlabeled data without human supervision. A sub-technique of unsupervised learning is clustering, which groups similar-looking data together, such as K-means clustering. Reinforcement learning relies on the machine receiving rewards based on actions to understand success.

Evaluation is the stage where the quality and performance of the created model are judged, scored, or evaluated. Each machine learning modeling technique has a corresponding evaluation technique. Classification problems use accuracy and the confusion matrix. Regression problems use root mean square error to evaluate numerical accuracy. Clustering problems use the silhouette method.

Deployment is the final stage where a high-quality model is moved from the lab out into the real world to solve real-world problems in production. Deployment can be implemented through various methods such as a mobile application, a website, or a cloud server, allowing actual users to take advantage of the completed work.
